What is missing everywhere: No ingredient layer with legal standing
How I know: Every skincare ontology I found stores ingredients as free text or a small hand-made list. The ONE knowledge graph that links cosmetic ingredients to EU law (TOXIN, Oxford, 2025) contains no products at all
What I do about it: Ingredients are individuals identified by their CosIng register entry, so regulatory status is INHERITED from the European Commission rather than asserted by me. 99.2% of products with a formula are linked
How strong is that claim: STRONGEST. Nobody has both halves. This is the thesis

What is missing everywhere: Nobody records where a claim came from
How I know: No reviewed skincare ontology says who asserted a claim or how much that source is worth. Every claim is presented as equally true
What I do about it: Every suitability claim is a Claim entity carrying its source, the exact sentence it was read from, the date, and one of four evidence levels. Specialised from PROV-O, a W3C standard
How strong is that claim: STRONG. The pattern exists elsewhere (O'Sullivan 2025), which is GOOD: I reuse rather than invent

What is missing everywhere: Everyone assumes you can buy the product
How I know: Every reviewed system recommends without asking whether the item is obtainable. In Lebanon that assumption fails, and it fails differently for imported and locally made products
What I do about it: Price in two currencies, per shop, with the date it was observed. Availability as a defined class. 11,937 products with at least one Lebanese shop
How strong is that claim: STRONG AND UNIQUE. No cosmetics system models purchasability

How I know: One of six reviewed skincare ontologies is publicly resolvable. The field cannot build on its own results
What I do about it: w3id address, WIDOCO documentation, Zenodo DOI, named methodology, and a FOOPS! FAIR score I actually measure
How strong is that claim: EASY AND RARE. Costs a week, and one in six competitors manages it

How I know: Rahayu et al. (2022), reviewing 28 ontology-based recommenders, found that NONE described an evaluation methodology. In my own set: two report satisfaction on under 30 people, one is a case study, one admits expert testing never happened
What I do about it: Four layers: structural (OOPS!, FOOPS!, OntoMetrics), functional (15 competency questions as SPARQL), logical (predicted vs inferred membership of six defined classes), comparative (the head-to-head sheet)
How strong is that claim: STRONG, and cheap. None of it needs users I do not have

What is missing everywhere: Nobody models what the user actually NEEDS
How I know: Concerns are modelled everywhere as an attribute of a product. AliCoCo (SIGMOD 2020) argues that leaves a semantic gap, because shoppers think in needs, not categories
What I do about it: Lebanese consumer needs as first-class entities: a routine under twenty dollars a month, one that survives a power cut, one buyable in a single pharmacy
How strong is that claim: MOST ORIGINAL, LEAST CERTAIN. Attempt it AFTER the four safe claims are delivered

What is missing everywhere: THE WHOLE ARGUMENT IN ONE SENTENCE

No system anywhere combines an ingredient layer with legal standing, a record of where each claim came from, and whether the product can actually be bought in the user's market. The one knowledge graph that links cosmetic ingredients to European regulation has no products in it. Every skincare ontology has products and no regulation. This thesis is the intersection, built for Lebanon, on 12,629 products.
